subsection: 10. Case study: the Apprentice Boys of Derry

notes.h: Background: Derry, the walls and the war of the two kings
notes.b: The Apprentice Boys exist to remember one event, the siege of Derry in 1688-89, and that event only makes sense against the planting of the city and the struggle between two kings.
points: Derry, formally called Londonderry, is a walled city on the River Foyle. It was planted (settled with colonists) by London companies in the early 1600s as a Protestant settlement, which is why it carries the 'London' name.
Nationalists tend to say Derry and unionists often say Londonderry, so the name itself shows the divide. This case study uses Derry.
The city walls were built between 1613 and 1619 and were never breached, so they gave Derry its distinctive fortified character and later became the focus of the parades.

In 1688 the Catholic King James II was deposed in the Glorious Revolution, and the Protestant William of Orange took the throne in 1689. James then tried to win back his thrones by fighting from Ireland, which produced the Williamite-Jacobite war (Jacobite means supporter of James).

The siege of Derry was part of that war. The Battle of the Boyne on 1 July 1690 followed it, and the Apprentice Boys must not be confused with the Orange Order, a separate loyal order that marks the Boyne on 12 July.
notes.tip: Examiners expect you to place the Apprentice Boys in context. Open with the siege and the war between James II and William, then link them to the later parades.

notes.h: The siege of Derry: the shutting of the gates and Lundy, 1688-1689
notes.b: The siege began with an act of defiance by young Protestants and was shaped by a quarrel over whether Derry should resist James II at all. Both episodes became central to later Protestant memory.
points: In December 1688 thirteen apprentice boys shut Derry's gates against a regiment loyal to James II. This 'Shutting of the Gates' is the event the apprentices' name comes from, and the thirteen became the organisation's symbol. This is why the thirteen apprentices are remembered as the first to resist.
Robert Lundy, the governor, was a Protestant who believed resistance was hopeless and favoured negotiating with James. The defenders distrusted him, and he left Derry in April 1689.

Lundy's name has become a byword for treachery in unionist tradition, which is why an effigy (a model figure) of him is burned each December. George Walker is the opposite figure: a defence leader remembered as a siege hero.
The siege proper began in April 1689 and lasted 105 days. George Walker and Henry Baker led the defence, and Baker died of fever during the siege.
Conditions inside the walls were terrible because the city was cut off. There was severe famine and disease, and the garrison ate horses, dogs and other animals to survive.
notes.tip: Keep the two events apart: the Shutting of the Gates was December 1688, while the Relief came in July-August 1689. A short-answer question may simply ask for the date of the shutting of the gates, so give December 1688.

notes.h: The relief of Derry and the symbols of the siege
notes.b: The siege ended when a supply ship broke the blockade of the river, and several objects from the siege became lasting symbols that the Apprentice Boys still use.
points: On 28 July 1689 the ships Mountjoy and Phoenix broke the boom (a barrier floated across the river to block ships) across the River Foyle, bringing food to the starving garrison.
The Jacobite army then withdrew. Sources vary on the exact day, so the safe way to date the lifting of the siege is late July to early August 1689.
The defenders flew a crimson (red) flag from the cathedral tower as a sign of defiance, and the cannon Roaring Meg on the walls became another symbol of the siege.
Together the walls, the crimson flag and Roaring Meg gave later generations physical things to display and commemorate, which is why flags, a cannon and the walls all feature in the parades.
The defence became a central Protestant story of resistance, a story reinforced the next year by the Boyne in 1690.
notes.tip: If you are asked what the August parade marks, answer the Relief (the lifting of the siege), not the shutting of the gates.

notes.h: The founding and organisation of the Apprentice Boys
notes.b: More than a century after the siege, Protestants in Derry formed a club to keep its memory alive. It grew into a wider organisation with its own headquarters.
points: The parent club, the Apprentice Boys of Derry club, was founded in 1814 in Derry to commemorate the siege. It was named after the apprentices who shut the gates in 1688, and members took the thirteen apprentices as their symbol.

Members were Protestant tradesmen and businessmen, and membership was open to Protestant men only, so this made the club part of the wider network of loyal Protestant bodies, so the organisation was socially respectable as well as Protestant.
The organisation spread beyond Derry through further clubs and branches, and it developed a central governing body, so a local club became a wider fraternal organisation.
The Memorial Hall in Society Street, opened in 1877, served as a memorial and headquarters and became the centre of the organisation's activities.
notes.tip: For an Ordinary Level paragraph, make sure you give 1814, who the members were, and the Memorial Hall in Society Street (1877); each correct, dated point earns marks.

notes.b: The Apprentice Boys mark the two key moments of the siege with two commemorations each year, and the rituals and the walls give them their character.
points: The August parade commemorates the Relief of Derry. It is traditionally held on 12 August and is now held on a Saturday near that date, and it is the largest Apprentice Boys event of the year.
The August parade follows a route round the city walls. Because the walls look down on the Bogside, a Catholic district just outside them, the route has a meaning beyond the commemoration itself.

The December commemoration marks the Shutting of the Gates and is held on a Saturday in December. It includes a service in St Columb's Cathedral (the Church of Ireland cathedral) and the burning of the Lundy effigy, a long-standing tradition.

Members wear crimson sashes and regalia, and the parades include bands, banners, a cannon fired in memory of the siege, crimson flags, wreaths for the dead and speeches. In the 2011 exam source, members also wore bowler hats.
Large crowds of members and visitors attend, which is why the events are as much a public spectacle as a private commemoration., so the August route round the walls was seen and heard by many people.
notes.tip: In a document question on the Apprentice Boys, describe what you see (uniform, ritual, religion, crowds) and add outside context such as the siege and the August route round the walls.

notes.h: Key concepts: tradition, identity, sectarianism and tolerance
notes.b: Four ideas from the syllabus help explain why a commemoration of events in 1688-89 could still matter so much in the twentieth century.
points: Cultural traditions are the distinct heritage, customs and public commemorations of each community. The Apprentice Boys' parades are a clear example of a tradition kept up by one community.
Cultural identity is a community's sense of belonging through shared history, symbols and commemorations. The siege story gave Protestant Derry a shared past to belong to.
Sectarianism is hostility between Protestants and Catholics based on religious identity and political allegiance. Critics argued that some displays of the siege story fed this hostility.

Tolerance and intolerance describe accepting or refusing the other community's identity and public displays. Disputes over parade routes were arguments about exactly this: whether each side would accept the other's right to be seen and heard.
notes.tip: Examiners want these key concepts used by name. Apply them to the parades, for example by calling the route past the Bogside a test of tolerance.

notes.b: For unionists the siege story stood for survival against the odds, but nationalists read the same symbols very differently.
points: Siege mentality is a term historians use for a community's sense of being surrounded and under threat. The story of 1688-89 reinforced this feeling among unionists, because it told them that survival depended on refusing to give way.
The slogan 'No Surrender' is the siege defiance slogan. It came to express defiance of Catholic and nationalist demands, and was used at parades and in political rhetoric.

For unionists the relief of 1689 represented the defence of Protestant civil and religious liberty against a Catholic monarch. Banners and slogans linked the siege to loyalty to the Crown and to the Protestant monarchy of 1689.
For nationalists the parades, and their route past the Bogside, symbolised a celebration of military conquest and of the Protestant ascendancy (the dominance of the Protestant minority).

Triumphalism is the word critics use for celebrations that display victory over another community. It was applied to the Apprentice Boys' parades because a victory over Catholic forces was being celebrated beside a Catholic district.
notes.tip: Give each side's reading of the same parade: heritage and liberty for unionists, triumphalism and provocation for nationalists, and name siege mentality and triumphalism.

notes.b: By the 1960s Derry was a city where the numbers and the power did not match, and the Apprentice Boys' route went through the middle of that tension.
points: Derry's population was majority Catholic, but unionists controlled the Londonderry Corporation (the city council) through gerrymandering, the drawing of ward boundaries to win more seats than votes justify. The boundaries were redrawn in the 1930s.
The Bogside lies just outside the walls, to the west, and was largely Catholic and working class. Other Catholic districts were the Creggan and the Brandywell.
Parades past the Bogside were a source of tension, and the route of the August parade was a recurring point of dispute. This is why the route became a recurring flashpoint.

Housing and voting grievances were raised by civil rights campaigners in Derry in 1968 and 1969. Nationalists saw the Apprentice Boys' parades as part of the city's unionist power structure, which linked the parades to the wider civil rights agenda.
notes.tip: When explaining why the 1969 parade mattered, link the Catholic majority, unionist control through gerrymandering, and the route past the Bogside.

notes.h: 12 August 1969 and the Battle of the Bogside
notes.b: The August 1969 parade is the best-known episode in the Apprentice Boys' history, because it led to rioting in Derry and to the arrival of the British army.
points: On 12 August 1969 the Apprentice Boys' parade marched along the walls near the Bogside, and clashes broke out between Bogside residents and the RUC (the Royal Ulster Constabulary, Northern Ireland's police).

Nationalists said the parade was a provocation. The Apprentice Boys said they were holding a legal, traditional march and that the disorder was started by others, so no single account of who began the stone-throwing can be given.
The Battle of the Bogside lasted from 12 to 14 August 1969. The RUC used CS gas (a tear gas) and residents built barricades.
The slogan 'Free Derry' was painted on a gable wall in January 1969, so it predates August. The barricades of August 1969 made the slogan a reality, and it became a symbol of nationalist resistance.
British troops were deployed in Derry on 14 August 1969, and in Belfast that evening. The events are seen as a turning point in the outbreak of the Troubles.
notes.tip: For cause and consequence, trace the chain: parade, clashes with the RUC, Battle of the Bogside, then army deployment. Do not confuse it with the siege of Derry or with Bloody Sunday in 1972, which are different events.

notes.h: Parades, restrictions and restoration in the 1970s
notes.b: After 1969 the parades became a security problem, and the wider conflict changed the city around the walls.
points: In some years of the early 1970s the authorities restricted or rerouted the parades because of violence, and the parades resumed as security improved.

The Apprentice Boys and their supporters argued that parades were a legitimate expression of their culture and loyalty, so restrictions felt to them like an attack on their identity. For example, the Walker Pillar was destroyed in 1973.
The IRA blew up the Walker Pillar, the monument to George Walker, on the city walls in 1973. It was a symbol of the siege, so its destruction was a symbolic attack on the tradition.
The organisation negotiated parade routes with the authorities and, later, with residents' groups, and this local dialogue and security planning kept the parades going.

The Protestant population of the west bank fell in the late 1960s and 1970s as many moved to the Waterside (the east bank of the Foyle). This reduced the Protestant presence on the west bank and deepened the sense of siege.
notes.tip: Say 'in some years of the early 1970s' for the restrictions, since no exact dates are needed, and show that routes were later negotiated.

notes.h: Case study: significance for unionists and nationalists
notes.b: The same parade could be a proud heritage event to one community and a painful display to the other. This is why it is such a useful case study of how a commemoration can take on contemporary political meaning.
points: For unionists the parades celebrate the defence of Protestant liberty, and they keep alive the memory of the siege as a foundation of loyalty.
For nationalists the parades are associated with the Protestant ascendancy and with the history of exclusion in the city.
The dispute over the parades was part of the wider civil rights agenda in Derry, linking cultural symbols to questions of discrimination and power, alongside housing and voting.
Both communities in Derry developed their own traditions, and the tension between them shaped the city's politics from the 1960s onwards.
Historians see the Apprentice Boys' tradition as an example of how a commemoration of a past event can take on political meaning in the present.
notes.tip: The 100-mark essay asks how far the Apprentice Boys contributed to cultural identity or were divisive. Give a stated judgement with detail from both communities and dated events (1688-89, 1814, 1877, 1969, 1970s).

notes.b: The events of 1969 and what followed left the Apprentice Boys at the centre of a divided city.
points: The 1969 parade and the Battle of the Bogside brought the civil rights crisis in Derry to a violent climax.
The events in Derry in 1969 led to British army deployment and to a sustained period of conflict in the city.
The Apprentice Boys retained a central place in Derry's civic and cultural life, and the Memorial Hall remained a focus of commemoration.
The disputes over parades and routes contributed to the lasting division between unionist and nationalist interpretations of Derry's history.
Major Apprentice Boys events continued to need police and security planning, which kept the parades in the public spotlight.
Unionists in the city worried about their place within the walls as Protestant numbers on the west bank fell during the Troubles.
notes.tip: Use the 1969 parade for cause and consequence questions: it led to the Battle of the Bogside and then to army deployment.

notes.b: Judging the Apprentice Boys means weighing a genuine commemorative tradition against its effect on a divided city, and recognising that each community judged it differently.
points: Achievement: the Apprentice Boys preserved a commemorative tradition that gave Protestant Derry a shared public identity over more than a century, an example of heritage and cultural expression.
Limit: the parades' route past the Bogside made them a point of conflict, and they became a symbol of division in the city.
Contemporary view: unionists regarded the parades as a legitimate expression of heritage and loyalty, and they resisted restrictions as an attack on their culture.
Contemporary view: nationalists saw the parades as triumphalist, and they argued that the route past the Bogside was a provocation.
Later view: historians stress that the tradition was both a genuine commemoration and a political statement, and that its meaning changed with the political conflict.
notes.tip: Judgement material that earns credit pairs achievement against limit and unionist against nationalist views, and contemporary against later views. State your own judgement.

keyTerms.definition: The distinct heritage, customs and public commemorations of the unionist and nationalist communities, which the Apprentice Boys' parades expressed in Derry.
A community's sense of belonging through shared history, symbols and commemorations, which the Apprentice Boys' memory of the siege reinforced for many unionists.
Hostility between Protestants and Catholics based on religious identity and political allegiance, which the disputes over the Apprentice Boys' parades reflected.
Tolerance is willingness to accept differing identities and commemorations, while intolerance is refusal to accept them, a central issue in disputes over the parades.
A community's sense of being surrounded and under threat, a term used by historians to describe the unionist attitude reinforced by the siege of Derry.
Celebration that displays victory over another community, a charge levelled by critics against the Apprentice Boys' parades.
The largely Catholic working-class area below the walls of Derry, which was central to the parade disputes and the events of 1969.
The lifting of the siege of Derry at the end of July and start of August 1689 after the relief ship Mountjoy broke the boom on the River Foyle, commemorated by the August parade.
Governor Robert Lundy, who favoured negotiating with James II in 1689 and whose name became a Protestant byword for betrayal.
The Apprentice Boys' headquarters in Society Street, Derry, opened in 1877.

factCards.definition: Apprentice boys in Derry shut the city gates in December 1688 against Jacobite forces loyal to James II.
The siege proper began in April 1689 and lasted about 105 days before it was lifted.
The relief ship Mountjoy broke the boom across the River Foyle on 28 July 1689, bringing supplies to the garrison.
The siege of Derry was lifted on 1 August 1689.
Robert Lundy was the governor who favoured negotiating with James II; he left the city in 1689 and his name became a byword for betrayal.
The city walls of Derry were built between 1613 and 1619.
The Apprentice Boys of Derry Club was founded in 1814 to commemorate the siege, and the Memorial Hall opened in 1877.
The Relief of Derry parade is held in August, traditionally on 12 August, and the Shutting of the Gates in December.
The Battle of the Bogside took place from 12 to 14 August 1969 after the Apprentice Boys' parade passed the Bogside.
The Bogside barricades of August 1969 gave rise to the name Free Derry, a symbol of nationalist resistance.
The Apprentice Boys' Memorial Hall in Society Street, Derry, opened in 1877 to honour the thirteen apprentice boys.

factCards.term: Siege mentality: who used the term
factCards.definition: Historians use the term siege mentality to describe the unionist sense of being surrounded and under threat.
An effigy of Governor Lundy is burned at the December commemoration, a custom said to date from 1832.
The IRA blew up the pillar commemorating George Walker on the city walls in 1973.
